edges.effect_quant: A 2024 meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials in 352 adults found no overall significant effect of oral glutamine on intestinal permeability (WMD -0.00, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.03), but a significant reduction appeared in studies using doses above 30 g/day; in a randomized 8-week trial of 106 adults with postinfectious IBS-D and increased permeability, glutamine reduced urinary lactulose/mannitol ratio from 0.11 to 0.05 and dramatically improved IBS severity versus placebo.
edges.population: adults receiving oral or enteral glutamine in trials measuring lactulose-mannitol ratios or related permeability markers, including postinfectious IBS-D and critically ill or surgical populations
edges.mechanism: Glutamine is a preferred fuel for enterocytes and may reinforce tight-junction integrity, reduce epithelial stress, and improve mucosal repair when the barrier is metabolically strained or inflamed.
edges.summary: Glutamine has a biologically plausible and partly trial-supported barrier-protective signal, but the literature is not uniformly positive. The cleanest conclusion is that glutamine can improve intestinal permeability in selected stressed or hyperpermeable states, while average effects across heterogeneous adult trials are more modest.
edges.caveats: Dose, route, baseline barrier dysfunction, and clinical context matter a great deal. Positive findings in postinfectious IBS-D or enteral-feeding settings do not guarantee benefit in every inflammatory or critical-care population.

evidence.notes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials on the effects of glutamine supplementation on gut permeability in adults.
